name: Pi prime chunks
spec:
Implement PiPrimeChunks(seed int64) (chunks []string, closestPrimes []int).

Calculate π to at least 99 digits after the decimal point. Start with π written in ordinary decimal notation, beginning with `3.`, then remove the decimal point. Use exactly the first 100 numeric digits, including the leading `3`. The digit string therefore contains the leading `3` followed by 99 digits that originally came after the decimal point. It must begin with `314159...` and contain no decimal point.

Split this 100-character digit string, in order, into chunks of either 2 or 3 digits. Use a deterministic pseudo-random generator created with `rand.New(rand.NewSource(seed))` from Go's standard `math/rand` package.

While more than 3 digits remain, call `rng.Intn(2)`. A result of `0` means choose a 2-digit chunk; a result of `1` means choose a 3-digit chunk. If that choice would leave exactly one digit remaining, use the other chunk size instead. When exactly 2 or 3 digits remain, use all remaining digits as the final chunk. Do not use time, package-level random functions, `crypto/rand`, or external state.

Return chunks as strings, preserving leading zeroes. A chunk made from the digits `0`, `6`, and `2` must be returned as `"062"`.

For each chunk, interpret its digits as a base-10 integer and find the closest prime number. Return those primes in closestPrimes at the matching indexes. The two returned slices must have the same length. A prime is an integer greater than 1 with no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. If two primes are equally close, return the smaller prime: the closest prime to `4` is `3`.

The function must not print anything. For the same seed, it must always return exactly the same chunks and closest primes.
